commentary.bottom_line: In the listed tests, external, temporal, or multisite validation often showed lower discrimination or shifted calibration compared with internal testing, such as an AUC of 0.886 falling to 0.786 on later data, though some models held steady or improved. The evidence suggests the practice reveals overestimated performance, but no study shows that it changes deployment decisions or patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: Tests are nonrandomized comparisons of internal with external, temporal, or multisite data, and none measures patient outcomes. One randomized trial among the hazard studies found sensitivity of 0.957 internally and 0.943 externally. External AUC fell from 0.886 to 0.786 in one test and rose from 0.847 to 0.870 in another. Inconsistency and indirectness support low certainty.

External checks surfaced errors that internal testing did not show. A stroke model kept an AUROC of 0.745 externally, but its observed-to-expected ratio was 0.12. An ICU model overestimated risk, with an intercept of -0.678. These results suggest that discrimination alone may hide calibration errors, which could mislead treatment thresholds.

One study found that leakage can arise in ordinary pipelines, when sibling recordings were split across sets and held-out patient labels entered few-shot exemplars. In another study, cluster grouping changed AUC by at most 0.0004, while withholding a whole region reduced it by 0.044 to 0.060. This suggests the unit of the split may matter most.

In Uganda and Kenya, AUROC was 0.81 for children under 5 but 0.62 for neonates. In another study, monolingual validation missed multilingual failures, and ICU parameter recall fell from 100.0% to 48.5%. These findings suggest that representative test data may need explicit strata for age and language.

FDA draft guidance links design validation to intended use under actual or simulated conditions, and FUTURE-AI asks that test data be separated from training data. A Canadian internal-external study found a pooled AUROC of 0.71 to 0.72 with substantial variation across hospitals. This suggests that site-level results may belong in submissions and purchasing reviews.

A prospective external validation at 18 centers enrolled 8,493 patients, and a Swedish deployment reviewed 74,679 records. These studies suggest that multisite validation is feasible at scale. No study reports the cost or staff time needed to obtain sequestered external data, so budgets for this practice would rely on local estimates.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares models validated only internally with models validated on sequestered external data in terms of deployment decisions, error rates after go-live, or patient outcomes. No study reports the cost of assembling representative test sets. No study defines a threshold for how closely test data must match the intended-use population.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One test used a cohort focused on racial and ethnic minorities and found miscalibration, and two hazard studies involved limited English or non-English populations, one of which found multilingual failures that monolingual validation missed. Health systems serving these groups therefore cannot assume that published external validation reflects performance in their patients and may need local testing.
